title: Deep Blue beats Kasparov
why: The first computer to beat a reigning world chess champion in a match.

title: AlexNet wins ImageNet
why: A neural net learns to recognize images far better than anything before it, and the deep learning era starts.

title: AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol
why: A machine wins at Go, the hardest board game, a decade before experts expected.

title: AlphaZero beats Stockfish
why: Teaches itself chess from scratch in hours, then beats Stockfish, the strongest chess engine.

title: AlphaFold wins CASP13
why: AI predicts the shapes of proteins better than any lab method in the field's main contest.

title: AI finds a new antibiotic
why: A neural network discovers halicin, which kills bacteria that resist existing drugs.

title: AlphaFold 2 solves protein folding
why: Predicting a protein's shape from its sequence, a 50-year-old problem in biology, is effectively solved.

title: AlphaFold maps the human proteome
why: The shapes of nearly every human protein, released free to every scientist.

title: AI controls fusion plasma
why: A neural network steers the superheated plasma inside a fusion reactor, a step toward fusion power.

title: AlphaTensor finds faster math
why: AI discovers ways to multiply matrices in fewer steps, beating a record that stood for 50 years.

title: GraphCast beats the best weather forecasts
why: Forecasts the weather ten days out more accurately than the world's leading system, in under a minute.

title: GNoME finds 380,000 new materials
why: AI discovers 2.2 million new crystals, about 800 years of discovery at the old pace.

title: FunSearch makes new math
why: A language model finds new answers to an open math problem, a first for an AI.

title: AlphaFold 3
why: Predicts how proteins, DNA and drug molecules fit together, which is how most drugs work.

title: AlphaProof wins IMO silver
why: AI solves olympiad math problems at the level of the world's best high school students.

title: AlphaEvolve breaks a 56-year-old record
why: AI finds a faster way to multiply matrices than the method mathematicians had used since 1969.

title: AI wins IMO gold
why: AI scores gold at the International Math Olympiad, the hardest math contest for students.

title: Erdős unit distance conjecture disproved
why: An AI finds what mathematicians missed for 80 years: points can have far more pairs exactly one unit apart than anyone believed.

title: Cycle double cover conjecture proved
why: An AI proves a 50-year-old conjecture about networks in under an hour, checked by computer.

title: Jacobian conjecture disproved
why: With Claude's help, a mathematician finds a one-line counterexample to an 87-year-old conjecture.

title: Ten open math problems settled
why: An AI resolves ten long-open problems at once, including whether every group can be approximated by finite ones.

title: Two-thirds of Riemann zeros proven on the line
why: Claude raises the share of zeros proven to follow the Riemann hypothesis from 41.6% to 67.2%, a record decades of human work had barely moved.

title: Navier–Stokes solution claimed
why: About 10,000 AI agents produce a computer-checked proof that fluid equations can break down, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems.

title: New CRISPR-like enzyme system
why: Claude agents comb 200,000 DNA-copying enzymes and spot a system no scientist had noticed, reminiscent of CRISPR.

title: 722 AI math papers, incl. quasi-Riemann
why: One release takes on hundreds of open problems, including what a Fields Medalist called the best result in his field in 100 years.

title: Yang–Mills existence proof claimed
why: AI proves the theories behind the strong nuclear force exist mathematically, part of a Millennium Prize problem.

title: Kakeya conjecture proved in every dimension
why: AI proves a central conjecture about how waves focus, settling the Kakeya conjecture in every dimension.

title: Exponential Time Hypothesis disproved
why: AI shows a core assumption behind hundreds of computer science papers is false.

title: Riemann hypothesis proved
why: Working with Claude, a mathematician proves the most famous open problem in math, posed in 1859, and computers confirm every step.
